note: 50 questions, all one level. Built for surprise while staying guessable. Every citation points at a source retrieved during research.

questions.prompt: How much food does the world throw away each year in shops, restaurants and homes?
questions.whyCorrect: 1.05 billion tons a year — thrown away while one in eleven people goes hungry.
questions.action: Weigh what your household bins in one week.

questions.prompt: How much food does the average person waste per year?
questions.whyCorrect: 132 kg — roughly your own body weight in food, binned every year, by every person on average.
questions.action: Compare 132 kg with your own weight.

questions.prompt: While the world wastes a billion tons of food, how many people go hungry?
questions.whyCorrect: 1 in 11 people are hungry, and 1 in 3 cannot afford a healthy diet. Hunger is a distribution problem, not a production problem.
questions.action: Ask why food is wasted in one place and scarce in another.

questions.prompt: How many people cannot afford a healthy diet?
questions.whyCorrect: 1 in 3 — around 2.8 billion people. They may get enough calories, but not enough nutrition.
questions.action: Price out a week of healthy meals where you live.

questions.prompt: What share of food is lost before it ever reaches a shop?
questions.whyCorrect: 13% is lost in harvest, storage and transport — on top of the 1.05 billion tons wasted at shops and homes.
whyWrong: Too high — but combined with retail waste, total losses approach a third.
questions.action: Ask what happens to crops with no refrigerated transport.

questions.prompt: What share of the world's greenhouse gases comes from wasted food?
questions.whyCorrect: 8–10% — if food waste were a country, it would be one of the world's biggest emitters. Growing, shipping and rotting food all release carbon.
questions.action: Ask what happens to food rotting in a landfill.

questions.prompt: What does food waste cost the world each year?
questions.whyCorrect: Over $1 trillion a year — money spent growing, shipping and storing food that nobody eats.
questions.action: Estimate what your family spends on food it throws out.

questions.prompt: Japan cut its food waste by how much?
questions.whyCorrect: 31% — and the UK cut 18%. Both prove that food waste is a solvable problem when a country decides to solve it.
questions.action: Look up one thing Japan did to cut food waste.

questions.prompt: The United Kingdom reduced food waste by:
questions.whyCorrect: 18% — solid progress, though behind Japan's 31%. Both used a mix of labelling changes, redistribution and public campaigns.
questions.action: Check the difference between 'use by' and 'best before'.

questions.prompt: How much electronic waste does the world produce each year?
questions.whyCorrect: 62 billion kg in 2022 — about 7.8 kg for every person alive, and heading for 82 billion by 2030.
questions.action: Count the electronic devices in your home.

questions.prompt: What share of e-waste is formally collected and recycled properly?
questions.whyCorrect: Only 22.3%. Over three quarters of the world's electronics are dumped, burned or dismantled by hand without protection.
questions.action: Find out where to recycle a phone near you.

questions.prompt: How much e-waste does each person generate per year?
questions.whyCorrect: 7.8 kg per person — and only 1.7 kg of that gets properly recycled.
questions.action: Weigh an old laptop and compare with 7.8 kg.

questions.prompt: How much e-waste per person is properly recycled?
questions.whyCorrect: Just 1.7 kg of the 7.8 kg generated. The rest contains gold, copper and rare metals that are simply lost.
whyWrong: That's the amount generated, not recycled.
Far more than is actually recovered.
questions.action: Look up what metals are inside a smartphone.

questions.prompt: By 2030, annual e-waste is projected to reach:
questions.whyCorrect: 82 billion kg — up from 62 billion in 2022. E-waste is growing far faster than recycling capacity.
questions.action: Ask why devices are replaced faster than they break.

questions.prompt: How much e-waste crosses international borders each year?
questions.whyCorrect: 5.1 billion kg is shipped abroad annually, and only 35% of that trade is formally controlled. The rest is largely unregulated.
whyWrong: It happens at massive scale despite treaties.
questions.action: Ask why a country would ship its waste elsewhere.

questions.prompt: What share of cross-border e-waste shipments are formally 'controlled'?
questions.whyCorrect: 35% — so roughly two thirds of the e-waste crossing borders moves outside proper regulation.
whyWrong: Too pessimistic — about a third is controlled.
questions.action: Look up the Basel Convention on waste shipments.

questions.prompt: How much new electrical equipment entered the market in 2022?
questions.whyCorrect: 96 billion kg — 50% more than in 2010. Every kilogram sold becomes waste eventually.
questions.action: Ask how long your last device lasted.

questions.prompt: New electrical equipment sales compared with 2010 are:
questions.whyCorrect: 50% more equipment enters the market than in 2010 — while proper recycling only reaches 22.3%.
questions.action: Ask what devices exist now that didn't in 2010.

questions.prompt: How much raw material does the world consume each year?
questions.whyCorrect: 113.6 billion tons in 2022 — up 23.3% from 92.1 billion in 2015. Consumption is accelerating, not slowing.
questions.action: Look up what 'domestic material consumption' counts.

questions.prompt: Material consumption grew how much between 2015 and 2022?
questions.whyCorrect: 23.3% in seven years — the world is pulling far more stuff out of the ground since the SDGs began, not less.
questions.action: Ask what 'decoupling growth from materials' means.

questions.prompt: How many tons of material does each person consume per year?
questions.whyCorrect: 14.2 tons per person, up from 12.4 in 2015 — roughly ten cars' worth of material per person per year, mostly sand, gravel and stone.
questions.action: Ask what makes up most of that 14.2 tons.

questions.prompt: Which material category is growing fastest?
options: Non-metallic minerals like sand, gravel and cement
questions.whyCorrect: Non-metallic minerals rose 39.0% — from 43.4 to 60.3 billion tons. The world's biggest material appetite is for concrete, not oil.
questions.action: Look at how much concrete is in one building near you.

questions.prompt: Which region increased material consumption the most since 2015?
options: Latin America and the Caribbean, up 132%
questions.whyCorrect: Latin America and the Caribbean more than doubled, up 132% — far beyond the global 23.3% rise.
whyWrong: Europe was not the fastest-growing region.
questions.action: Ask what drives a doubling of material use.

questions.prompt: Sand, gravel and cement consumption rose from 43.4 to:
questions.whyCorrect: 60.3 billion tons — a 39% jump. Sand is now the second most-consumed resource on Earth after water.
questions.action: Look up why the world is running short of usable sand.

questions.prompt: Fossil fuel material consumption grew how much since 2015?
questions.whyCorrect: 6.2% — the slowest-growing category, and a genuine sign that energy transition is starting to bite.
questions.action: Compare 6.2% for fossil fuels with 39% for minerals.

questions.prompt: Biomass consumption — crops, timber, fish — grew how much since 2015?
questions.whyCorrect: 11.8% — faster than fossil fuels or metals, driven by food and construction timber for a growing population.
questions.action: Rank the four material categories by growth.

questions.prompt: The world's material footprint grew how much between 2015 and 2022?
questions.whyCorrect: 21.3% — the footprint counts everything extracted to make what a country consumes, including materials mined abroad.
questions.action: Ask why a country's footprint can exceed what it mines.

questions.prompt: How many sustainable consumption policies exist worldwide?
questions.whyCorrect: 530 policies in 71 countries as of 2024 — up 6% in a year. Real momentum, though only about a third of countries participate.
questions.action: Find one sustainability policy your country has.

questions.prompt: How many countries have sustainable public procurement policies?
questions.whyCorrect: 67 countries, up from 40 in 2020. Governments are enormous buyers, so what they choose to purchase shifts whole markets.
questions.action: Ask what your school or council buys most of.

questions.prompt: What share of the world's 250 largest companies publish sustainability reports?
questions.whyCorrect: 96% — near-universal. The question now is whether the reports are accurate, not whether they exist.
questions.action: Find a big company's sustainability report online.

questions.prompt: Sustainability reporting grew how much between 2016 and 2023?
questions.whyCorrect: Nearly four times as many reports — driven by investor pressure and new rules, not voluntary goodwill alone.
questions.action: Ask what makes a company report honestly.

questions.prompt: What share of Minamata Convention parties (on mercury) nominated national focal points?
questions.whyCorrect: 94% — treaty participation on hazardous chemicals is genuinely strong, with 82% also filing national reports.
questions.action: Look up what mercury does to the human body.

questions.prompt: Reporting compliance under the Montreal Protocol on ozone-damaging chemicals is:
questions.whyCorrect: 100% — every party reports. The Montreal Protocol is the most successful environmental treaty ever signed.
questions.action: Look up what happened to the ozone hole.

questions.prompt: How many countries filed Stockholm Convention reports on persistent pollutants?
questions.whyCorrect: 91 countries in 2022. 'Persistent' pollutants are chemicals that don't break down — they accumulate in bodies and food chains for decades.
questions.action: Look up one persistent organic pollutant.

questions.prompt: 1.05 billion tons of food wasted, while 1 in 11 go hungry. This shows:
options: The world doesn't grow enough food
The world grows enough food but distributes and stores it badly
questions.whyCorrect: There is more than enough food. It is lost in transport, priced out of reach, or thrown away — which makes hunger a solvable logistics and income problem.
whyWrong: Production exceeds need — waste proves it.
Japan and the UK show waste can be cut deliberately.
questions.action: Find out if a food redistribution charity operates near you.

questions.prompt: Only 22.3% of e-waste is properly recycled. The main risk of the rest is:
options: Toxic metals like lead and mercury leach into soil and water, often burned by informal workers
questions.whyCorrect: Informal dismantling often means burning plastic off wires by hand, releasing lead, mercury and dioxins into people and groundwater.
whyWrong: Volume is the least of the problem.
questions.action: Look up what happens at an informal e-waste site.

questions.prompt: Material consumption per person rose from 12.4 tons to:
questions.whyCorrect: 14.2 tons — a 14.8% rise per person, on top of population growth. Both multipliers are pushing in the same direction.
whyWrong: The rise was larger than this.
questions.action: Ask what happens when both population and per-person use rise.

questions.prompt: What share of the world's top 100 companies report on sustainability?
questions.whyCorrect: 79% of top-100 national companies, against 96% of the global top 250 — smaller firms report less.
whyWrong: Reporting is high but not universal at this level.
questions.action: Ask why bigger companies report more than smaller ones.

questions.prompt: Basel Convention reporting on hazardous waste hit its target of:
questions.whyCorrect: The 70% target was met in 2020, with 107 parties reporting in the 2023 cycle. Tracking hazardous waste is the first step to controlling it.
whyWrong: Full compliance was not the target.
questions.action: Ask why a country might not report its waste exports.

questions.prompt: The average person wastes 132 kg of food yearly. Over a decade that's:
questions.whyCorrect: About 1.32 tons per person per decade — the weight of a small car, in food thrown away by one individual.
whyWrong: Ten times too low for a single year.
questions.action: Multiply 132 kg by everyone in your household.

questions.prompt: Why does food waste matter for climate as well as hunger?
options: Growing, transporting and rotting wasted food produces 8-10% of all greenhouse gases
questions.whyCorrect: Every wasted meal carries the emissions of the land, water, fuel and fertiliser used to produce it — plus methane when it rots in landfill.
whyWrong: The climate link is one of the largest single levers available.
Rotting food releases methane, a potent greenhouse gas.
questions.action: Look up how much water it takes to grow one loaf of bread.

questions.prompt: 'Circular economy' means:
options: Designing products so materials get reused rather than dumped after one life
questions.whyCorrect: Instead of extract-make-discard, materials circulate: repaired, remanufactured, recycled. With only 22.3% of e-waste recovered, the world is far from circular.
whyWrong: The shape of buildings is unrelated.
A circular economy reduces new consumption.
questions.action: Find something you own that could be repaired instead of replaced.

questions.prompt: Metal ore consumption grew 7.4% since 2015 while minerals grew 39%. This suggests:
options: Metals are being used less overall
Construction is driving material demand more than manufacturing
questions.whyCorrect: Sand, gravel and cement are construction materials — the world is building at a scale that dwarfs its growth in metal use.
whyWrong: Metal use still grew, just more slowly.
questions.action: Count the construction sites you passed this week.

questions.prompt: Sustainable public procurement grew from 40 countries in 2020 to:
questions.whyCorrect: 67 countries — a 68% rise in two years. Public purchasing is one of the fastest-moving levers in Goal 12.
questions.action: Ask what your government's biggest purchases are.

questions.prompt: E-waste grows from 62 to 82 billion kg by 2030 while recycling stays near 22%. That means:
options: The absolute amount of unrecycled e-waste will grow substantially
questions.whyCorrect: A constant percentage of a growing total means more waste, not less. Recycling capacity has to grow faster than consumption just to stand still.
whyWrong: The gap is projected to widen.
Recycling rates have not kept pace with sales.
questions.action: Calculate 22% of 62 billion and of 82 billion.

questions.prompt: Which environmental treaty has 100% reporting compliance?
questions.whyCorrect: The Montreal Protocol on ozone-depleting substances — universal participation and full reporting, which is why the ozone layer is healing.
questions.action: Look up when the ozone layer is expected to fully recover.

questions.prompt: Japan cut food waste 31% and the UK 18%. The lesson is:
options: National policy and public campaigns produce measurable reductions
questions.whyCorrect: Both countries changed labelling, redistribution rules and public habits — and the waste figures moved. It is a policy problem with known solutions.
whyWrong: Two countries have already demonstrated large cuts.
Food loss is severe in lower-income countries too, mostly before retail.
questions.action: Suggest one rule that would cut waste in your school canteen.

questions.prompt: The 'material footprint' differs from 'material consumption' because it:
options: Counts materials extracted anywhere to make what a country consumes
questions.whyCorrect: A country can look clean while importing goods whose mining happened elsewhere. The footprint follows the material back to the ground.
whyWrong: It has nothing to do with shoes.
questions.action: Trace where the metal in your phone was mined.

questions.prompt: Material consumption rose 23.3% while world population rose far less. This means:
options: Each person is using more, not just that there are more people
questions.whyCorrect: Per-person consumption rose 14.8%, from 12.4 to 14.2 tons — so rising appetite accounts for most of the increase, not just more people.
questions.action: Compare 23.3% total growth with 14.8% per-person growth.

questions.prompt: The clearest Goal 12 contradiction is:
options: 1.05 billion tons of food wasted while 1 in 11 people go hungry
questions.whyCorrect: Enough food is produced for everyone, yet a billion tons is binned while 700+ million go hungry. Goal 12 is about the gap between plenty and access.
whyWrong: Consumption is rising faster than the planet can supply.
questions.action: Plan one meal this week that uses leftovers.
